const rad = (deg) => (deg * Math.PI) / 180;
const mercY = (lat) => Math.log(Math.tan(Math.PI / 4 + rad(lat) / 2));

function project({ lat, lon }) {
  const x = W / 2 + scale * (rad(lon) - rad(pin.lon));
  const y = H / 2 - scale * (mercY(lat) - mercY(pin.lat));
  return [x, y];
}

const [px, py] = project(pin);

const svg = `<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${H}">
  <rect width="${W}" height="${H}" fill="#e6e6e6"/>
  <circle cx="${px}" cy="${py}" r="5" fill="#111111"/>
</svg>`;
writeFileSync("map.svg", svg);

project is a Mercator projection centered on the pin. Longitude maps straight to x. Latitude goes through mercY first, which stretches it toward the poles so that shapes keep their proportions. The scale of 2300 means the 720 pixel canvas covers about 18 degrees of longitude, which is enough to show a region and its nearest cities.

To draw the map, run the script:

node map.mjs

Open map.svg in a browser. You should see a light gray rectangle with a black dot in the exact center.

It is not a map yet, but every later step is this same function applied to more points.

Draw the land

A dot on a gray rectangle could be anywhere. Next, add the coastline so the dot has something to sit on. Replace the import line at the top of the file with these two:

import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { feature } from "topojson-client";

Then add this below the const [px, py] line:

const world = JSON.parse(
  readFileSync("node_modules/world-atlas/land-50m.json", "utf8"),
);
const land = feature(world, world.objects.land).features[0];

function ringPath(ring) {
  const points = ring.map(([lon, lat]) =>
    project({ lat: Math.max(-85, Math.min(85, lat)), lon }),
  );
  return points
    .map(([x, y], i) => `${i ? "L" : "M"}${x.toFixed(1)} ${y.toFixed(1)}`)
    .join("") + "Z";
}

const landPath = land.geometry.coordinates
  .flatMap((polygon) => polygon.map(ringPath))
  .join("");

Each coastline in the file is a ring of coordinates. ringPath runs every point through project and joins the results into an SVG path. The clamp to 85 degrees is there because mercY goes to infinity at the poles, and Antarctica reaches one.

Once that is in place, draw the path. Add this line to the SVG template, between the rect and the circle:

  <path d="${landPath}" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#999999" stroke-width="0.7"/>

Run the script again. The dot now sits in a wide stretch of land, with the Atlantic at the left edge, the Mediterranean at the bottom, and the Adriatic on the right.

The pin is Chamonix for a reason. FieldRank's UTMB Mont-Blanc page draws the same spot as server-side SVG, so you have a finished version to compare against as you go. That page uses d3-geo for the projection and clipping instead of the hand-written versions here, and adds a few layers this tutorial leaves out.

Draw only what is in view

The picture is right and the file is wrong. Check its size:

ls -l map.svg

It is about 880 KB. The script projected every coastline on Earth and wrote all of it into the path, and the browser then threw away everything outside the frame. For a picture that is 720 pixels wide, that is the whole budget of a page spent on Antarctica.

The fix is to cut each ring down to the frame before writing it. Add this above ringPath:

const BLEED = 6;

function clipEdge(points, axis, limit, keepBelow) {
  const inside = (p) => (keepBelow ? p[axis] <= limit : p[axis] >= limit);
  const out = [];
  points.forEach((cur, i) => {
    const prev = points[(i + points.length - 1) % points.length];
    if (inside(cur) !== inside(prev)) {
      const t = (limit - prev[axis]) / (cur[axis] - prev[axis]);
      out.push([
        prev[0] + t * (cur[0] - prev[0]),
        prev[1] + t * (cur[1] - prev[1]),
      ]);
    }
    if (inside(cur)) out.push(cur);
  });
  return out;
}

function clipRing(points) {
  let out = clipEdge(points, 0, -BLEED, false);
  out = clipEdge(out, 0, W + BLEED, true);
  out = clipEdge(out, 1, -BLEED, false);
  return clipEdge(out, 1, H + BLEED, true);
}

This is the Sutherland-Hodgman algorithm. clipEdge walks around a ring and keeps the points on the inside of one straight line. Where the ring crosses the line, it adds a new point exactly on the crossing. clipRing does that four times, once for each side of the frame.

The cut is made 6 pixels outside the frame, not at it. Clipping closes each shape along the cut, and that new edge takes the coastline stroke like any other. Cut at the frame and you get a gray line down the side of the map wherever land runs off it. Cut a little outside and the false edge is hidden.

Next, replace ringPath with a version that clips after projecting:

function ringPath(ring) {
  const points = clipRing(
    ring.map(([lon, lat]) =>
      project({ lat: Math.max(-85, Math.min(85, lat)), lon }),
    ),
  );
  if (points.length < 3) return "";
  return points
    .map(([x, y], i) => `${i ? "L" : "M"}${x.toFixed(1)} ${y.toFixed(1)}`)
    .join("") + "Z";
}

A ring that ends up with fewer than three points is entirely out of view, so it returns nothing.

Run the script and check the size again. The map looks identical, and the file is now about 2.5 KB.

Add the cities

With the land drawn, you can tell the pin is somewhere in western Europe. A few city names will make it specific. Start by adding a list of cities below landPath. The population is there for a later step:

const cities = [
  { name: "Milan", lat: 45.46, lon: 9.19, pop: 1370000 },
  { name: "Turin", lat: 45.07, lon: 7.69, pop: 850000 },
  { name: "Lyon", lat: 45.76, lon: 4.84, pop: 520000 },
  { name: "Geneva", lat: 46.2, lon: 6.14, pop: 200000 },
  { name: "Grenoble", lat: 45.19, lon: 5.72, pop: 158000 },
  { name: "Lausanne", lat: 46.52, lon: 6.63, pop: 140000 },
  { name: "Bern", lat: 46.95, lon: 7.45, pop: 134000 },
  { name: "Annecy", lat: 45.9, lon: 6.13, pop: 130000 },
  { name: "Monza", lat: 45.58, lon: 9.27, pop: 123000 },
  { name: "Novara", lat: 45.45, lon: 8.62, pop: 104000 },
];

Then turn each city into a small dot with its name beside it:

function cityMark(name, x, y) {
  return `<circle cx="${x.toFixed(1)}" cy="${y.toFixed(1)}" r="2" fill="#555"/>
  <text x="${(x + 6).toFixed(1)}" y="${(y + 3.5).toFixed(1)}" font-family="monospace" font-size="10" fill="#555">${name.toUpperCase()}</text>`;
}

const cityMarks = cities
  .map((city) => {
    const [x, y] = project(city);
    return cityMark(city.name, x, y);
  })
  .join("\n  ");

Each city goes through the same project function as the pin, so it lands in the right place without any extra math. The label starts 6 pixels to the right of the dot. The 3.5 added to y lowers the text so that its middle lines up with the dot, not its baseline.

Next, add ${cityMarks} to the SVG template on its own line, after the path and before the pin's circle. Run the script again. You should see ten gray dots, each with its name in capitals.

Two things are wrong. Annecy's name is printed straight across the pin, which is the one thing the map exists to show. And near Milan, three names are stacked into something unreadable. Take the pin first.

Run labels away from the pin

Annecy sits 30 pixels left of the pin, so a label that runs to the right has nowhere to go but through it. The rule that fixes this is short: a label goes on the side of its dot that faces away from the pin.

Replace cityMark and cityMarks with:

function cityMark(name, x, y, left) {
  const tx = left ? x - 6 : x + 6;
  const anchor = left ? "end" : "start";
  return `<circle cx="${x.toFixed(1)}" cy="${y.toFixed(1)}" r="2" fill="#555"/>
  <text x="${tx.toFixed(1)}" y="${(y + 3.5).toFixed(1)}" text-anchor="${anchor}" font-family="monospace" font-size="10" fill="#555">${name.toUpperCase()}</text>`;
}

const cityMarks = cities
  .map((city) => {
    const [x, y] = project(city);
    return cityMark(city.name, x, y, x < px);
  })
  .join("\n  ");

text-anchor="end" tells SVG that the x you gave is where the text stops, so the name grows leftward from its dot. The last argument, x < px, is the whole rule: a city left of the pin gets a label that runs left.

Run it. Annecy, Geneva, Lausanne, Lyon, and Grenoble now read leftward, and the pin has clear space on every side.

Milan is still a mess, and this rule cannot help. All three of those cities are on the same side of the pin.

Stop labels landing on each other

This is the hard part, and the answer is less clever than you might hope. Node has no font to measure text with, so you estimate the box each label will fill, and you leave out any label whose box hits one that is already there.

Start with the two helpers. Add them below cityMark:

const CHAR_W = 6, HALF_H = 6, MARGIN = 4;

function textBox(name, x, y, left) {
  const w = name.length * CHAR_W;
  const x0 = left ? x - 6 - w : x + 6;
  return { x0, x1: x0 + w, y0: y - HALF_H, y1: y + HALF_H };
}

function overlaps(a, b) {
  const apartX = a.x1 + MARGIN <= b.x0 || b.x1 + MARGIN <= a.x0;
  const apartY = a.y1 + MARGIN <= b.y0 || b.y1 + MARGIN <= a.y0;
  return !(apartX || apartY);
}

textBox guesses the rectangle a name will cover. A 10 pixel monospace font draws each character about 6 pixels wide, so the width is the letter count times six. That estimate is the reason the labels use a monospace font: every name's width is known without measuring anything.

overlaps treats two boxes as clear only when they are apart by the margin on at least one axis. The margin matters. Two labels that miss each other by a pixel are technically separate and still read as one smudge.

Once those are in, replace cityMarks with a version that checks before it draws:

const taken = [{ x0: px - 5, x1: px + 5, y0: py - 5, y1: py + 5 }];

const cityMarks = [...cities]
  .sort((a, b) => b.pop - a.pop)
  .map((city) => {
    const [x, y] = project(city);
    const left = x < px;
    const text = textBox(city.name, x, y, left);
    const dot = { x0: x - 2, x1: x + 2, y0: y - 2, y1: y + 2 };
    if (taken.some((box) => overlaps(box, text) || overlaps(box, dot))) {
      return "";
    }
    taken.push(text, dot);
    return cityMark(city.name, x, y, left);
  })
  .filter(Boolean)
  .join("\n  ");

taken starts with one box in it, the pin, so no label can land there either. The cities are sorted by population, largest first, which decides who wins: Milan claims its space before Monza and Novara get a turn. Each city that fits adds both its text box and its dot to the list. Each city that does not fit returns an empty string and is left off the map.

Run the script one more time. Milan stands alone, and eight of the ten cities are left.

Leaving labels out has a cost. Sometimes nothing survives, and sometimes there was nothing to begin with. The Hardrock 100 starts in Silverton, Colorado, and no large city falls inside its frame. Its map names two peaks in place of cities. Whatever rule you write for cities needs an answer for the empty case.

The whole script

Here is map.mjs in one piece:

import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { feature } from "topojson-client";

const W = 720, H = 190;
const pin = { lat: 45.92, lon: 6.87 }; // Chamonix
const scale = 2300; // pixels per radian

const rad = (deg) => (deg * Math.PI) / 180;
const mercY = (lat) => Math.log(Math.tan(Math.PI / 4 + rad(lat) / 2));

function project({ lat, lon }) {
  const x = W / 2 + scale * (rad(lon) - rad(pin.lon));
  const y = H / 2 - scale * (mercY(lat) - mercY(pin.lat));
  return [x, y];
}

const [px, py] = project(pin);

const world = JSON.parse(
  readFileSync("node_modules/world-atlas/land-50m.json", "utf8"),
);
const land = feature(world, world.objects.land).features[0];

const BLEED = 6;

function clipEdge(points, axis, limit, keepBelow) {
  const inside = (p) => (keepBelow ? p[axis] <= limit : p[axis] >= limit);
  const out = [];
  points.forEach((cur, i) => {
    const prev = points[(i + points.length - 1) % points.length];
    if (inside(cur) !== inside(prev)) {
      const t = (limit - prev[axis]) / (cur[axis] - prev[axis]);
      out.push([
        prev[0] + t * (cur[0] - prev[0]),
        prev[1] + t * (cur[1] - prev[1]),
      ]);
    }
    if (inside(cur)) out.push(cur);
  });
  return out;
}

function clipRing(points) {
  let out = clipEdge(points, 0, -BLEED, false);
  out = clipEdge(out, 0, W + BLEED, true);
  out = clipEdge(out, 1, -BLEED, false);
  return clipEdge(out, 1, H + BLEED, true);
}

function ringPath(ring) {
  const points = clipRing(
    ring.map(([lon, lat]) =>
      project({ lat: Math.max(-85, Math.min(85, lat)), lon }),
    ),
  );
  if (points.length < 3) return "";
  return points
    .map(([x, y], i) => `${i ? "L" : "M"}${x.toFixed(1)} ${y.toFixed(1)}`)
    .join("") + "Z";
}

const landPath = land.geometry.coordinates
  .flatMap((polygon) => polygon.map(ringPath))
  .join("");

const cities = [
  { name: "Milan", lat: 45.46, lon: 9.19, pop: 1370000 },
  { name: "Turin", lat: 45.07, lon: 7.69, pop: 850000 },
  { name: "Lyon", lat: 45.76, lon: 4.84, pop: 520000 },
  { name: "Geneva", lat: 46.2, lon: 6.14, pop: 200000 },
  { name: "Grenoble", lat: 45.19, lon: 5.72, pop: 158000 },
  { name: "Lausanne", lat: 46.52, lon: 6.63, pop: 140000 },
  { name: "Bern", lat: 46.95, lon: 7.45, pop: 134000 },
  { name: "Annecy", lat: 45.9, lon: 6.13, pop: 130000 },
  { name: "Monza", lat: 45.58, lon: 9.27, pop: 123000 },
  { name: "Novara", lat: 45.45, lon: 8.62, pop: 104000 },
];

function cityMark(name, x, y, left) {
  const tx = left ? x - 6 : x + 6;
  const anchor = left ? "end" : "start";
  return `<circle cx="${x.toFixed(1)}" cy="${y.toFixed(1)}" r="2" fill="#555"/>
  <text x="${tx.toFixed(1)}" y="${(y + 3.5).toFixed(1)}" text-anchor="${anchor}" font-family="monospace" font-size="10" fill="#555">${name.toUpperCase()}</text>`;
}

const CHAR_W = 6, HALF_H = 6, MARGIN = 4;

function textBox(name, x, y, left) {
  const w = name.length * CHAR_W;
  const x0 = left ? x - 6 - w : x + 6;
  return { x0, x1: x0 + w, y0: y - HALF_H, y1: y + HALF_H };
}

function overlaps(a, b) {
  const apartX = a.x1 + MARGIN <= b.x0 || b.x1 + MARGIN <= a.x0;
  const apartY = a.y1 + MARGIN <= b.y0 || b.y1 + MARGIN <= a.y0;
  return !(apartX || apartY);
}

const taken = [{ x0: px - 5, x1: px + 5, y0: py - 5, y1: py + 5 }];

const cityMarks = [...cities]
  .sort((a, b) => b.pop - a.pop)
  .map((city) => {
    const [x, y] = project(city);
    const left = x < px;
    const text = textBox(city.name, x, y, left);
    const dot = { x0: x - 2, x1: x + 2, y0: y - 2, y1: y + 2 };
    if (taken.some((box) => overlaps(box, text) || overlaps(box, dot))) {
      return "";
    }
    taken.push(text, dot);
    return cityMark(city.name, x, y, left);
  })
  .filter(Boolean)
  .join("\n  ");

const svg = `<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${H}">
  <rect width="${W}" height="${H}" fill="#e6e6e6"/>
  <path d="${landPath}" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#999999" stroke-width="0.7"/>
  ${cityMarks}
  <circle cx="${px}" cy="${py}" r="5" fill="#111111"/>
</svg>`;
writeFileSync("map.svg", svg);

To see what the map adds to a page, compress it the way a web server would and count the bytes:

gzip -c map.svg | wc -c

Where this stops working

The text is part of the drawing, so it scales with it. On a phone 360 pixels wide, this map renders at half size and the 10 pixel labels become 5 pixel labels. Fixing that means taking the names out of the SVG and positioning them as HTML over it, which is its own tutorial.

The label boxes also lean on the font. They assume a monospace face about 6 pixels per character. A different font, or names in another language, throws the estimate off and labels can overlap again.

The placement is greedy. A label that does not fit is dropped, when trying the other side of its dot or the row above might have saved it.

And a map is more than a coastline and some cities. The Western States 100 map has Lake Tahoe beside the pin and the Sierra Nevada named above it, and neither is in this script.

Both are less work than they look, because every step here has been the same three moves: load some shapes or points, run them through project, and decide what fits. A lake is a path like the land, filled with the water color. Natural Earth publishes lakes as their own file, separate from world-atlas. A range name is a label like a city, with one more box in taken. That is the next thing to build.

articles.title: I wrote 187 tests for a Chrome extension. The three bugs that mattered were invisible to all of them.
articles.description: My unit tests were green. My integration tests were green. The feature was broken in a way that...
articles.body_html:
My unit tests were green. My integration tests were green. The feature was broken in a way that produced no error, no warning, and no visual clue that anything was wrong.

The feature was a CSS difference blend mode, used to compare a design mockup against a live page: matching pixels turn black, so only the differences light up. Mine turned nothing black. It looked exactly like normal mode, and I lost about a week to it.

The cause was one line of CSS, and the reason no test caught it is the interesting part.

1. The blend mode that silently did nothing

Here is the overlay, simplified. A closed shadow root holds an image positioned over the page:

#overlay-host {
  position: absolute;
  z-index: 2147483647;   /* stay above the page */
}

.overlay-image {
  mix-blend-mode: difference;
}

That looks fine. It is not.

mix-blend-mode blends an element with its backdrop — but only within its own stacking context. And z-index on a positioned element creates a stacking context. So the host became a sealed box, and the image blended against the empty space inside that box instead of against the page underneath.

The result isn't an error. It isn't even visibly wrong unless you know what difference should look like. The image just renders normally, as though you never set the property.

The same applies to opacity below 1, filter, transform, isolation, backdrop-filter, mask, contain: paint and will-change of any of those. Any one of them on an ancestor silently disables blending. On a page you don't control — which is the entire premise of a browser extension — any of them might arrive from the site's own CSS.

The fix was to stop creating a stacking context on the host and move z-index onto the children that actually need it:

#overlay-host {
  position: absolute;
  /* No z-index, transform, opacity, filter, isolation or contain here:
     any of them creates a stacking context and silently kills blending. */
  z-index: auto;
}

.overlay-image {
  z-index: 2147483646;
  mix-blend-mode: difference;
}

Plus a MutationObserver re-pinning those properties inline with !important, because hostile page CSS will try to set them back.

Why no test caught it: every assertion I had was of the form getComputedStyle(img).mixBlendMode === 'difference'. That was true the entire time. The property was set. It was applied. It just had nothing to blend with. Computed style tells you what the engine parsed, not what the compositor drew.

The test that caught it samples actual pixels:

// Red block under a red overlay in difference mode must composite to black.
const px = await pixelAt(screenshot, 120, 160);
assert(px[0] < 12 && px[1] < 12 && px[2] < 12,
  `expected black, got rgb(${px})`);

That one assertion would have saved me the week.

2. The licence that never expired

Different flavour of invisible. This one lied to the user's face.

The extension has a paid tier backed by licence keys. Validation looked like this:

async function validateLicense(key, instanceId) {
  const res = await fetch(VALIDATE_ENDPOINT, { /* ... */ });
  const payload = await res.json();

  if (res.ok && isValid(payload)) {
    await storage.set({ isPro: true, /* ... */ });
    return { ok: true, isPro: true };
  }

  return { ok: false, error: messageFrom(payload) };   // ← writes nothing
}

Spot it? The success path writes to storage. The failure path returns an error object and touches nothing.

So when a subscription lapsed and the key was disabled, pressing Re-check in the UI did this:

  • called the API
  • got back valid: false, status: "disabled"
  • displayed "This license key is disabled." to the user
  • left isPro: true in storage

The customer read an accurate error message while keeping every paid feature. The only thing that ever revoked access was a once-per-24-hours background revalidation, so a cancelled subscriber kept Pro until their browser happened to check again.

Why no test caught it: my test suite faked the paid tier by writing isPro: true straight into storage. Every test of a Pro feature started from "pretend they're Pro". Nothing ever ran the activation path. I had thorough tests of what Pro users could do and zero tests of how someone becomes — or stops being — a Pro user.

Finding it meant buying my own product. I made a real subscription purchase in the payment provider's test mode, activated the key, then disabled it from the dashboard and watched what the extension actually did. The fix:

/* A definite "no" about the key this browser is running on: revoke now.
   Only ever on a real answer from the API - offline and unconfigured results
   say nothing about the key and must never downgrade anyone. The key must
   match the stored one too, so typing someone else's dead key into the box
   cannot strip a paying customer of Pro. */
await revokeIfCurrentKey(key, status || 'invalid');
return { ok: false, error: messageFrom(payload) };

Those three guards are the whole problem in miniature. "Revoke on failure" is a one-line change that would also have logged out every customer whose wifi dropped.

3. The SVG that rendered at 240×150

A user drops in an SVG mockup. It renders at roughly a quarter of its real size.

SVGs exported without width and height attributes — just a viewBox — have no intrinsic size. Load one into an <img> and ask for naturalWidth, and you get a placeholder. Here is Chrome 152, measured:

SVG naturalWidth × naturalHeight
width="480" height="320" 480 × 320
viewBox="0 0 640 400" only 240 × 150
no dimensions, no viewBox 300 × 150

That 240 is the giveaway. CSS says a replaced element with no intrinsic size falls back to a default object size of 300×150 — but when there's a viewBox, there is an intrinsic ratio, so the browser keeps the 150 height and derives the width from it: 150 × (640/400) = 240.

Which means the wrong size scales with your design's aspect ratio. It isn't a constant you'd notice as obviously bogus. It's a plausible-looking number that happens to be a quarter of the truth, and it changes per file. That's why it read as "my positioning maths is off" rather than "the dimensions are wrong".

The fix is to stop asking the <img> and read the file:

function measureSvg(text) {
  const svg = new DOMParser()
    .parseFromString(text, 'image/svg+xml').documentElement;
  if (!svg || svg.nodeName !== 'svg' || svg.querySelector('parsererror')) return null;

  const plain = (v) => {
    const m = /^\s*([\d.]+)\s*(px)?\s*$/.exec(v || '');
    const n = m ? parseFloat(m[1]) : NaN;
    return Number.isFinite(n) && n > 0 ? n : null;
  };

  const w = plain(svg.getAttribute('width'));
  const h = plain(svg.getAttribute('height'));
  if (w && h) return { width: Math.round(w), height: Math.round(h) };

  const box = (svg.getAttribute('viewBox') || '').trim().split(/[\s,]+/).map(Number);
  if (box.length === 4 && box[2] > 0 && box[3] > 0) {
    return { width: Math.round(box[2]), height: Math.round(box[3]) };
  }
  return null;
}

Note plain() rejects width="100%" and width="10em" — percentage and relative units aren't a pixel size, and treating them as one is the same bug with extra steps.

The pattern

All three bugs share a shape: the code did exactly what it said, and the result was still wrong.

  • The blend mode was applied — to the wrong backdrop.
  • The licence check returned the correct answer — and discarded it.
  • The image loaded successfully — at a size nobody asked for.

Not one threw. Not one logged. Every assertion I had about state passed, because the state was right. The outcome was wrong, and outcomes live in rendered pixels, in persisted storage after a round trip, and in what a real file actually contains.

So the harness samples all three. It drives a real Chrome over the DevTools Protocol — no npm packages, just Node's WebSocket client speaking CDP — loads a deliberately hostile test page that tries to break the overlay with !important rules, and then reads pixels back out of real screenshots:

const chrome = spawn(chromePath, [
  `--load-extension=${EXT_DIR}`,
  `--remote-debugging-port=${PORT}`,
  '--enable-unsafe-extension-debugging',
  '--force-device-scale-factor=1',
]);

const { data } = await cdp.send('Page.captureScreenshot', { format: 'png' }, session);

The hostile page is worth the effort on its own. It sets display: none !important on the overlay host, plus z-index, isolation and transform — the exact properties that killed the blend mode. Writing the attack into the fixture means the regression can't come back quietly.

187 tests now, across four suites. The ones that earn their keep aren't the ones asserting that a function returns what it returns. They're the handful that look at what actually came out the other end.

These came out of building PixelMatch, a Chrome extension that overlays your design on the live page and scores how closely the build matches. Free to install.

articles.title: I IPO'd my GitHub profile. You can buy shares in me.
articles.description: My GitHub profile is a stock now. It's called $VJK, it trades in rupees during Indian market hours,...
articles.body_html:
My GitHub profile is a stock now. It's called $VJK, it trades in rupees during Indian market hours, and anyone with a GitHub account can buy or sell it. My commits decide what it's worth.

vineetjk (Vineet J Karni) · GitHub

Best things need time! . vineetjk has 80 repositories available. Follow their code on GitHub.

github.com

Where this came from

Over the last few weeks I kept running into posts here on DEV where people had turned their GitHub profile into something completely different. Giorgi built a cyberpunk console with a city made out of his contributions. Someone turned theirs into a roguelike dungeon, someone else into a spaceship mission console, and there's a Minecraft tree that grows from your commits.

I loved all of them. My own profile README at that point was empty. I had cleaned it up and never put anything back.

I wanted to make one too, but I didn't want to build another city or another game. What I liked about those posts is that each profile says something about the person who made it. So I asked myself what mine would say. The honest answer is that I spend a lot of my free time reading about markets and finance.

So I listed myself on the stock market.

What's on the profile

From top to bottom:

  • A ticker that scrolls the price, the fair value and the latest market news.
  • A quote panel with the price, the day's open, high, low and volume, and how far the price can still move today.
  • A daily candlestick chart. The dashed orange line is the "fair value" my commits give the stock.
  • Four buttons: buy 5, buy 25, sell 5 and sell 25.
  • The top shareholders and the latest trades.
  • My GitHub numbers, shown like a company's fundamentals. My languages show up as "sector allocation".

It follows your GitHub theme, so light mode users get a light version.

How a trade works

There's no website and no server. Trading happens through GitHub issues.

When you click BUY 5, GitHub opens a new issue in my profile repo with the title BUY 5 $VJK already filled in. You can change the number to anything from 1 to 25. Click Create, and that's your order.

Opening the issue starts a GitHub Actions workflow. It reads the title, checks the order and fills it. If it's your first trade, you get ₹10,000 of play money to start with.

Every share you buy pushes the price up 0.15%, and you pay the price after your own push. $VJK listed at ₹55.10, so buying 5 shares at that price goes like this:

  • the price moves from ₹55.10 to ₹55.50
  • you pay ₹55.50 × 5 = ₹277.50
  • you're left with ₹9,722.50 in cash and 5 shares

The bot then redraws the images on my profile, commits them, leaves a receipt on your issue and closes it. This is the receipt for that exact trade:

✅ Filled · BUY 5 $VJK @ ₹55.50
Fill price (after your own impact) ₹55.50
Order value ₹277.50
Your trade moved the price ▲ +0.73%
Your position 5 shares, avg ₹55.50
Cash ₹9,722.50
Portfolio value ₹10,000.00 (+0.00%)

Selling is the same thing in reverse. Each share you sell pushes the price down 0.15%, and you get the price after your push. If you sold those 5 shares ten minutes later and nobody else had traded, the price would drop back to ₹55.10 and you'd get ₹275.50. You'd be down ₹2.

That's on purpose. If you could buy and sell straight away without losing anything, someone would write a script to pump the price and dump it.

A few other rules:

  • One order every 10 minutes per person.
  • If you try to sell more than you have, it sells what you have. If you have nothing, the order is rejected.
  • If you don't have enough cash, you get as many shares as you can afford.
  • Bots can't trade, and neither can I.

Market hours and limits

The market keeps Indian market hours: 09:15 to 15:30 IST, Monday to Friday. If you place an order outside those hours, it waits. The bot comments that it's queued, leaves the issue open, and fills it at the next morning's open. Indian brokers call this an after-market order (AMO). Closing the issue cancels it.

The price can't move more than 10% from the previous day's close. When it hits the upper limit, buying stops for the rest of the day, and when it hits the lower limit, selling stops. Indian exchanges call this a circuit. Here it also stops one person with ₹10,000 from doubling the price in an afternoon.

Prices move in steps of ₹0.05, and big amounts use Indian digit grouping, so you'll see ₹1,00,000.00 and not ₹100,000.00.

How my commits move the price

This is my favourite part. Every weekday at 15:33 IST, right after the close, the workflow looks at my contributions from the last 30 days and works out a fair value:

export function fairValue(contrib30, cfg) {
  const value = cfg.listingPrice * Math.sqrt((contrib30 + 10) / (cfg.baseline30 + 10));
  return snap(Math.round(value * 100), cfg.tickPaise);
}

A normal month for me is about 30 contributions, and that's worth ₹100 a share. A month with nothing drops it to ₹50. The square root is there so one crazy day doesn't make the number explode, and the + 10 keeps a quiet month from taking it to zero.

Then the closing price moves 20% of the way toward that fair value, still inside the 10% limit. So during the day you decide the price, and at the close my commits pull it back toward what they say it's worth.

Commits I make at night or on weekends still count. They stay in the 30-day window, so the next weekday close picks them up, and they keep counting for 30 days.

A chart from day one

A brand new stock would start with an empty chart. So when $VJK listed, it backtested the previous 70 trading days: start at ₹100 and run every close as if the market had already existed, using my real contribution history.

The chart is pretty honest about my year. I was busy in July, and the price climbed to ₹174. I didn't push anything public in August or September, and it slid all the way down to ₹50. Then I made 30 contributions on October 4th, and the last session before listing closed right at its +10% limit.

So $VJK listed at ₹55.10, with a fair value of ₹101.25. If I keep committing, it should keep climbing for a while.

Dividends

Every time one of my pull requests gets merged, everyone holding shares gets ₹2 per share. It's a small reason to hold instead of flipping.

What it looks like with traders

This one is from a local rehearsal. I ran two and a half weeks of made-up trading through the same code, with fake usernames, to see how the leaderboard and the chart look once people are actually trading. The real market starts empty.

How it's built

Everything on the profile is an SVG

GitHub doesn't run JavaScript in a README, and it strips <style> tags. But an SVG loaded through <img> can carry its own CSS, including animations. So every panel is an SVG. The ticker scrolls, the market status dot pulses, and the buy and sell buttons have a shine that sweeps across them. A link can only wrap a whole image, which is why each button is a separate file.

SVGs shown this way can't load anything external either, not even Google Fonts. So I embedded JetBrains Mono, cut down to just the characters I use. That comes to about 5 KB per weight. JetBrains Mono has no ₹ sign, so the rupee comes from a 628-byte cut of Noto Sans Mono, which has the same character width. Avatars get downloaded and embedded too.

For dark and light mode, the README uses <picture>:

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="assets/dark/quote.svg?v=f3a9c1d2e0">
  <img src="assets/light/quote.svg?v=8b2e4a7c91" width="100%" alt="...">
</picture>

The ?v= part is a hash of the file. GitHub caches images, so when a panel changes, the README points at a new URL.

One workflow for everything

The workflow runs at the opening bell, at the closing bell, and every time someone opens an issue with VJK in the title:

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "47 3 * * 1-5" # 09:17 IST
    - cron: "3 10 * * 1-5" # 15:33 IST
  issues:
    types: [opened]
  workflow_dispatch:

Every run does the same job: fetch my GitHub stats, ring whichever bell is due, settle every open order, redraw the SVGs, regenerate the README, then commit and push. The receipts only go out after the push works, so nobody gets a receipt for a trade that isn't in the ledger.

The ledger is just data/market.json in the repo, and its git history is the full record of every trade.

Things I had to work around

GitHub cancels queued runs. With a concurrency group, GitHub keeps one run going and one waiting, and cancels the rest. If ten people order at once, most of those runs never happen. So no run belongs to a single issue. Each run settles every open order, and whichever run survives does the work of the cancelled ones.

Queued runs start from an old commit. A waiting run checks out the commit from when it was triggered, which can be behind what the previous run just pushed. Checking out the branch name instead fixes that, and if a push still gets rejected, the job resets to the new tip and runs the tick again.

Bursts and rate limits. Every order costs two API calls, a comment and a close, and GitHub limits how fast a bot can create content. So each run settles at most 20 orders. If more are waiting, it triggers itself again with workflow_dispatch, one of the few events a workflow's own token is allowed to start.

Issue titles are user input. Anyone can open an issue with any title. Here the title only ever gets matched against a regex in Node. It never goes into a shell command and never gets written into the README. rudratosh wrote a good post on what profile automation workflows can expose, and it's worth reading before you build one of these.

No empty commits. Rendering is deterministic. If nothing changed, the files come out byte for byte the same and the workflow skips the commit.

The bot's commits aren't mine. They're authored by github-actions[bot], so trading can't inflate my contribution graph, and through it, my own stock price.

No dependencies

It's plain Node with no npm packages. The market itself is a pure function of the current state, my stats and the time, which made it easy to test. 29 tests cover the rules, the rendering and a full run of the workflow script against fixtures.

Try it

Go buy some $VJK on my profile. The market's open 09:15 to 15:30 IST on weekdays, and orders placed outside those hours wait for the next morning.

If you want your own stock, the code is in the same repo. scripts/README.md has the steps: change the symbol and the username, and set how many contributions a normal month is for you.

I'm curious who ends up as the biggest shareholder.
